cases.caseName: Safeco Insurance Co. of America v. Burr
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: For FCRA civil liability, a willful violation can include reckless disregard; the Court described recklessness as conduct creating an unjustifiably high risk that is known or so obvious it should be known.
cases.operationalUse: Do not label an error willful merely because it persisted; preserve the dispute history and repeated notice facts, and leave liability conclusions to counsel.
cases.limits: The case arose from adverse-action notices in insurance pricing and does not make every inaccurate tradeline willful.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: A statutory violation alone does not necessarily establish concrete Article III injury for damages; dissemination of misleading OFAC alerts supported concrete reputational harm for affected class members, while undisseminated internal files did not establish that same harm on the stipulated record.
cases.operationalUse: Track whether inaccurate information was actually disclosed and any concrete consequences, without implying that documentation proves liability.
cases.limits: This is primarily a federal standing decision; it is not a general rule that an undisseminated inaccuracy never matters for correction or other relief.

cases.caseName: Department of Agriculture Rural Development Rural Housing Service v. Kirtz
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The FCRA's civil-liability provisions waive federal sovereign immunity for a federal agency that qualifies as a person under the Act.
cases.operationalUse: Do not reject a supported dispute solely because the furnisher is a federal agency; preserve the source and status of the government account.
cases.limits: The decision addressed federal sovereign immunity, not whether the reporting in a particular consumer's case is inaccurate or what damages are available.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
cases.holding: Section 1681e(b) does not create a categorical factual-versus-legal threshold. The relevant question is whether the asserted inaccuracy is objectively and readily verifiable; a live issue requiring bespoke legal reasoning may fall outside that test.
cases.operationalUse: Classify a proposed dispute by the exact field and supporting document, and distinguish a readily checkable mismatch from an unresolved legal interpretation.
cases.limits: Binding in the Second Circuit only; the decision remanded and did not establish that every contract-related disagreement is actionable.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.holding: A furnisher's section 1681s-2(b) investigation may not be unreasonable or cursory, and its scope depends on the specific information in the CRA notice. An omission can be inaccurate or incomplete when it creates a materially misleading impression, including failure after investigation to report a bona fide dispute in the circumstances addressed.
cases.operationalUse: Draft precise bureau disputes that identify the field, evidence, and why the presentation is materially misleading; do not treat a generic disagreement notation as automatic relief.
cases.limits: Binding in the Ninth Circuit only; the opinion distinguishes initial furnisher duties from duties triggered after CRA notice and does not validate meritless disputes.

cases.caseName: Hinkle v. Midland Credit Management, Inc.
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
cases.holding: On the mistaken-identity debt-buyer record, a reasonable jury could find a furnisher's investigation inadequate when it merely compared the disputed data with the same internal electronic data and did not obtain available account-level documentation.
cases.operationalUse: For a genuine not-mine dispute, ask for objective identity/account evidence and identify why rechecking the same source would not resolve the mismatch.
cases.limits: Binding in the Eleventh Circuit only and fact-specific; the app must never suggest identity theft or a not-mine claim without the user's truthful factual basis.

cases.caseName: Marchisio v. Carrington Mortgage Services, LLC
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
cases.holding: A furnisher's investigation was unreasonable on an extreme record where its systems repeatedly failed to incorporate settlements showing no balance and it reverified a nonexistent balloon payment despite detailed notice.
cases.operationalUse: Preserve prior resolution documents and repeated dispute results; surface contradictions between a settlement or court record and the reported balance for user verification.
cases.limits: Binding in the Eleventh Circuit only and based on unusually extensive repeated notice; it does not make any single verification error reckless or willful.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
cases.holding: After a consumer pinpointed a post-bankruptcy mortgage inaccuracy, the CRA could not establish as a matter of law that simply forwarding the dispute to the furnisher and accepting its response was a reasonable reinvestigation on that record.
cases.operationalUse: For bankruptcy-related entries, compare the exact reported balance, past-due amount, responsibility, dates, and court documents instead of asserting that every reference to a discharged debt must disappear.
cases.limits: Binding in the Eleventh Circuit only and fact-specific; bankruptcy discharge and credit reporting require exact order and tradeline review, and unresolved bankruptcy-law questions must go to counsel.
